extracted.intended_audience: criminalists, judges, lawyers, forensic psychologists, and legal scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing perception, inference, statistics, and knowledge in criminal investigation and court work, including common cognitive errors, the role and limits of statistics, and the physiological/psychological bases of testimony. Intended to guide evaluation of witnesses, evidence, and expert consultation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aprioristic mistakes (Natural prejudices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tacit assumptions and natural prejudices lead many people to make errors because they assume the order of nature and the order of knowledge are identical; certain classes of people are taken as better or worse than average and this prejudice affects judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively fight natural prejudices; be aware that impressions from sensation are instinctive and difficult to destroy; do not let fixed impressions (e.g., preconceived notions of guilt) trump reflective reconsideration. Example: the moon-at-horizon illusion and persistence of initial impressions in criminal trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistakes in observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors arising from faulty or incomplete sensory observation (to be discussed under sense-perception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that observational mistakes are distinct from logical fallacies and require scrutiny of sensory conditions, witness acuity, and circumstances of observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistakes in generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: When the facts are right but the inferences are wrong, often because the environment or accompanying circumstances unduly influence inference—i.e., judgments drawn from context rather than the object itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hasty generalization from environment alone; extract the fact in itself from its environment and study it without accompanying circumstances before using environment as a means of proof. Examples: assuming a Tanagra is genuine because it's in a connoisseur's house; assuming a tramp's watch is stolen because of his appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistakes of confusion (Ambiguity of terms or association errors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors due to unclear representation of what proof is, ambiguous words, or careless compounding of concepts and symbols with objects or events that should not have been united.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify concepts and avoid uncritical association of terms with objects; beware inferences drawn from ambiguous wording (e.g., mistaken inferences from the phrase 'identical motive'). Logical petitio or ignoratio errors belong here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical fallacies (syllogistic mistakes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Purely logical mistakes in reasoning or syllogism which can lead to incorrect legal conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish these formal logical errors from observational or conceptual mistakes and correct via formal analysis of reasoning steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extract facts from their environment before inferring
rubrics_metrics.description: The environment is a means of proof but not a proof itself; inferences drawn solely from environment tend to bury errors deep within an inferential system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validate the object or event in itself first, then adduce environmental circumstances as successive means of proof; failure to do so makes later detection of the error difficult or impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistics are valid for large numbers, not individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical laws have validity when dealing with great numbers; constant regularity becomes perceptible only with numerous cases, while single cases show many variations and exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use population-level regularities (Quetelet, circle analogy) for broad inference but avoid over-applying statistical generalizations to explain or determine individual cases. Example: death-rates inform insurers but tell an individual little about their specific life-span.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistics must connect quantities with qualities to be useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminological statistics that deal only with quantities are of limited scientific value; meaningful statistics should relate quantitative data to qualities (motives, education, previous life) to derive psychological or causal insights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure statistical collection and analysis include qualitative dimensions (motives, background, cause) and not merely counts of arrests/sentences; only then will statistics begin to have real scientific value for criminal psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware bureaucratic/statistical incompleteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Official criminal statistics are often complete in tabulation but lack psychologically valuable material (e.g., motive, basis for sentences, prior life) because they are governed by statutes and legal processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically assess official reports for missing qualitative information; where possible, supplement with targeted data collection focusing on motives, education, sentencing rationales, and prior life to render statistics interpretable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of certainty required depends on practical consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of evidence and certainty required to claim 'we know' varies according to whether the verdict will have significant practical consequences; higher stakes demand more stringent proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be more rigorous about declaring knowledge when practical consequences are large (e.g., medical, legal policy) and accept less absolute assertions in domains with low practical impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge as relative/subjective truth; assert modestly
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge is consciousness of definite content but not identical with objective truth; criminalists should claim only relative truth and be ready to reconsider as conditions change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit assertions to what is justifiable given current information; maintain institutions (revision, retrial) that recognize the provisional character of legal knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Found knowledge upon the largest possible number of experts
rubrics_metrics.description: An event is known only when all who possess special knowledge of its type have spoken; criminalists must base their knowledge on the input of relevant specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult appropriate experts before judging matters requiring special information; do not attempt to decide technical issues without expert assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study physiological psychology of the senses to determine trustworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: To ascertain the nature, influence, trustworthiness and relation of sense-perception to objects we must study the physiological psychology of senses as it applies to judge, jury, witness, and accused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate findings from physiological psychology (Helmholtz, Fechner, Weber) into evaluation of testimony and perception; do not treat sensory reports as unproblematically veridical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess witness knowledge of relevant physical laws (optics, acoustics, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceptions are influenced by knowledge of physical principles (reflection of sound, refraction of light, optics); ignorance or knowledge of such laws alters how a person interprets sensory input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating testimony about visual or auditory events, determine whether the witness understands relevant physical laws; use relational interrogation to establish whether they attended to or know such principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptions are rarely pure—identify admixtures of imagination/judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceptions are commonly mixed with imaginations, judgments, efforts, and volitions; sensation alone is only one component of the perceptual content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe witnesses to separate raw sensory content from immediate judgments or imaginations; be skeptical of testimony where perception appears heavily suffused with interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contradictions among witnesses as corrective
rubrics_metrics.description: Contradictions between testimonies serve as a safeguard against trusting the same untruth repeated; absence of contradiction often indicates lack of sufficient starting points for further examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value and investigate contradictions rather than dismiss them; where testimony is uniformly concordant, inquire whether similar training/ignorance produced the same error rather than assuming truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess perceptive skill and apperception speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceptive power varies with individual skill; rapid and comprehensive apperception is characteristic of more capable observers and affects the amount and quality of what is perceived in short observation times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider measures of apperception and the witness's demonstrated observational skill when weighing testimony; compare descriptions from observers of differing skill before concluding one is untrue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for individual differences of nature and nurture in perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceptions vary with an individual's nature (innate) and nurture (learning); each person's sensory apparatus and prior experience shape their perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximate a witness's intellectual and experiential background and adapt evaluation accordingly; do not treat all witnesses as perceptually equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of vicariousness/substitution of the senses (cross-modal imagery)
rubrics_metrics.description: One sense may substitute for another in representation: repeated auditory exposure to a voice can conjure a face in imagination, and imagined visual details may be reported as perceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish actual multimodal perception from cross-modal imagination; question whether reported visual detail could be an imagined construct triggered by prior sounds or partial impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply modern psychophysical laws (e.g., Weber's Law) to evaluate sensory reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychophysical principles (summation of stimuli, Weber's Law about increments of sensation) are relevant to understanding how stimulus intensity maps to sensation and perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established psychophysical laws to interpret claims about differences or thresholds in perception (e.g., changes in loudness/brightness), and to test plausibility of sensory reports.
